identity.title: Food Safety Plan (Preventive Controls for Human Food) – Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips, Salem Plant
identity.issuer: Willamette Valley Foods, Inc. (prepared by Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager and PCQI)
identity.site: Salem — 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301

page_refs.agencies: page 7, section 9 (FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture named)

scan.summary: This is the company's own written food safety plan. It is the main document FDA looks at under the Preventive Controls for Human Food rule (21 CFR Part 117). It covers the hazard analysis, preventive controls, monitoring, corrective actions, verification, and a short supply-chain section for the Salem hummus and bean dip line. It is your document, not the agency's, so the gaps below are yours to fix. This reading found the same gaps as the earlier one: no recall plan, a supply-chain program that is too thin, no validation or reanalysis, controls that are listed but not monitored, and no signature from the owner or agent in charge. It also found one new gap in how cooling is monitored.
scan.freshness_note: The plan took effect 2025-05-12 and is about 16.5 months old. That is inside the 3-year reanalysis cycle, so age alone is not the problem. But the plan is unsigned and has open gaps. Ask whether a signed or revised version exists. If one does, it should replace this copy on file. Inferred from 21 CFR 117.170(a): reanalysis is due no later than 2028-05-12, or sooner if products, process or suppliers change.

gaps.title: Supply-chain program is too thin
gaps.description: Section 8 has one approved-supplier sentence. It does not say which hazards the supplier controls (for example Salmonella in tahini, or stones in beans), what verification activity applies (on-site audit, sampling and testing, or record review) or how often. It also does not cover how suppliers get approved, how verification is documented, what happens when a supplier fails, or the records required. A third-party certificate and a COA do not meet the rule on their own unless they are tied to a named hazard and a determined verification activity.
gaps.fix: Write a full supply-chain program under Subpart G. List each raw material whose hazard is controlled before receipt. Name the supplier control, the verification activity and its frequency (an annual onsite audit is the default for SAHCODHA hazards such as Salmonella in tahini). Add written approval procedures, receiving procedures, corrective action for supplier non-conformance, and the record list.
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

gaps.title: Refrigerated storage hazard has no preventive control
gaps.description: The hazard analysis marks Listeria growth in refrigerated storage as needing a preventive control. Section 4 has no control, limit, monitoring or corrective action for it: no storage temperature limit, no cooler monitoring, and no response to a temperature excursion. The 45-day shelf life is also not supported by anything that limits growth, such as a pH limit, a preservative, or a shelf-life study (inferred).
gaps.fix: Add a refrigeration process control. For example, product held at or below 41°F, cooler temperature monitored continuously or at set intervals, a corrective action for excursions that includes evaluating the product, and verification. Record the basis for the 45-day shelf life (formulation pH or preservative, and challenge or shelf-life study data).
gaps.locator: Section 3 (page 3) identifies it; missing from sections 4–6
gaps.quote: Refrigerated RTE product with a 45-day shelf life

gaps.title: Salmonella in ingredients added after the cook step is not analyzed
gaps.description: The hazard analysis treats the bean cook as the kill step for the finished product. But tahini, garlic, lemon juice, spices and olive oil are blended in after the cook and never go through it. Tahini and spices are known sources of Salmonella. That hazard is not evaluated.
gaps.fix: Add a hazard analysis row for each ingredient added after the cook. Evaluate Salmonella (and Listeria where relevant). Name the control: a supplier control under the supply-chain program, a validated process at the supplier, or a control at this plant.
gaps.quote: Cook step is the kill step for the finished product

gaps.title: Chemical hazards other than sesame not evaluated
gaps.description: The only chemical hazard in the analysis is sesame. The plan does not consider pesticide residues or mycotoxins in beans and sesame seeds, sanitizer or chemical residues, undeclared allergens in the spice blends, or radiological hazards.
gaps.fix: Add chemical hazards to the hazard analysis for each ingredient and step. Record whether each needs a preventive control and why.

gaps.title: No written recall plan
gaps.description: The plan identifies hazards that need preventive controls (Listeria, sesame, metal), so it must include a written recall plan. There isn't one. The plan does not cover notifying customers or the public, effectiveness checks, or what happens to recalled product.
gaps.fix: Add a recall plan covering: who is responsible, how consignees in OR, WA and ID are notified, public notice when needed, effectiveness checks, and disposition of recalled product. Reference the date-code and lot-tracing records.

gaps.title: Environmental monitoring procedure is incomplete
gaps.description: The plan says 10 Listeria spp. sites weekly in zones 1 and 2. It does not name the sites, say when during production they are swabbed, name the test method or laboratory, or include zone 3 and 4 sites. The rule expects written procedures that identify locations, number of sites, timing, the test and the lab.
gaps.fix: Write an environmental monitoring procedure with a site map, site list by zone, timing (for example, mid-shift, at least 3 hours into production), test method, lab, and corrective action escalation by zone.
gaps.quote: Listeria spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2

gaps.title: Records review leaves out calibration, testing and supplier records
gaps.description: The PCQI review covers monitoring records and nothing else. It does not include thermometer calibration records, finished product test results, environmental monitoring results, or supplier verification records. The rule requires those to be reviewed within a reasonable time.
gaps.fix: Extend section 7 so the PCQI also reviews calibration, product testing, environmental monitoring and supplier verification records within a set time, and signs them.
gaps.quote: The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven working days of their creation.

gaps.title: No reanalysis schedule or triggers
gaps.description: The plan does not say it will be reanalyzed at least every 3 years. It also does not list what triggers an earlier reanalysis: a change in process or product, new hazard information, an unanticipated problem, or a preventive control found to be ineffective.
gaps.fix: Add a reanalysis section with the 3-year cycle (by 2028-05-12 at the latest), the triggers, and who performs or oversees it (the PCQI).

gaps.title: Corrective actions skip root cause and product evaluation
gaps.description: The cause is recorded only for cook failures. Most corrective actions do not require finding and fixing the cause, preventing recurrence, evaluating the affected product for safety, and keeping affected product out of commerce. For example, after an ATP failure or a label mismatch, product already made is not evaluated.
gaps.fix: For each corrective action, add: identify and correct the cause, take steps to prevent recurrence, evaluate affected food, and prevent adulterated food from entering commerce. Record each step.
gaps.quote: All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed by the PCQI within seven days.

gaps.title: Allergen label check at printing and on the line not monitored
gaps.description: Section 4 says labels are reviewed at receipt and at printing. Monitoring covers receipt only. Nothing checks that the right label is at printing or on the line during a run or at changeover.
gaps.fix: Add monitoring of the label at printing and on the line, at start-up and at each product changeover, with a record and a corrective action.
gaps.quote: The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs the label log.

gaps.title: No corrective action for unanticipated problems
gaps.description: The plan has no procedure for problems it did not foresee: a control that turns out not to be properly implemented, one found to be ineffective, or a situation with no written corrective action. Such a procedure must include a reanalysis decision.
gaps.fix: Add a general corrective action procedure for unanticipated problems. Include evaluating the product, fixing the cause, and deciding whether to reanalyze the plan.

gaps.title: Finished product testing: no procedure and no response to a positive
gaps.description: Monthly Listeria monocytogenes testing is mentioned. There is no written procedure (sampling plan, number of samples, lot definition, test method, lab) and no corrective action if a result comes back positive (hold, lot disposition, investigation, possible recall).
gaps.fix: Write a product testing procedure. Add a corrective action for a positive result, including holding the lot pending results and deciding on disposition or recall.
gaps.quote: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory.

gaps.title: No validation of the cook and cooling limits
gaps.description: The cook limit and the cooling limits are process controls, but nothing shows they have been validated with scientific or technical evidence. Also inferred, and worth checking: Salem sits at a low elevation where water boils just under 212°F. In an open kettle, an internal temperature of at least 212°F may not be physically reachable. If so, the limit would fail on paper every batch, or the records would not reflect reality.
gaps.fix: Have the PCQI gather or run validation for the cook (for example, a heat penetration study or published lethality data) and for cooling (for example, FDA Food Code or published C. perfringens data), before or shortly after implementation. Check the cook limit against what the kettle can actually reach and restate it if needed.

gaps.title: Stones in dry beans have no working control
gaps.description: The hazard analysis says stones are controlled at metal detection and by supplier screening. A metal detector does not detect stones. Supplier screening does not appear in the supply-chain program as a supplier control.
gaps.fix: Name a real control: an in-house destoner or sorting step with monitoring, or a supplier control under Subpart G with verification. Correct the justification in section 3.

gaps.title: Sesame cross-contact washdown checked only by ATP, and scheduling not monitored
gaps.description: ATP measures general organic residue, not sesame protein. Running hummus last in the day is not monitored or recorded. Nothing confirms the full washdown took place before the next non-sesame run.
gaps.fix: Add monitoring and a record for the production schedule and the washdown. Verify washdown with a sesame-specific allergen test (for example, a lateral-flow or ELISA swab), and add a corrective action if it fails.
gaps.quote: washdown verified by ATP swab before the next non-sesame product

gaps.title: Plan not signed and dated by the owner, operator or agent in charge
gaps.description: The approval line names a job title only. There is no name, signature or date. The rule requires the plan to be signed and dated by the owner, operator or agent in charge when first done and whenever it is modified.
gaps.fix: Have the owner, operator or agent in charge sign and date the plan. Do it again after each revision.

gaps.title: Cooling monitoring does not record when cooling starts
gaps.description: The cooling limits run from 135°F. Monitoring records temperatures at 2 hours and 6 hours but does not record the time and temperature when the batch reached 135°F. Without that starting point, the record cannot show the limit was met.
gaps.fix: Record the start time and temperature (the point product reaches 135°F), plus the 2-hour and 6-hour readings, on the cooling log.
gaps.citation: 21 CFR 117.145 (I believe this applies; the adequacy of monitoring is a judgment call)
gaps.quote: The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling log.

deadlines.title: Probe thermometer calibration
deadlines.source_line: Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly

deadlines.title: Metal detector manufacturer service
deadlines.source_line: the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually

deadlines.title: Finished product Listeria monocytogenes test
deadlines.source_line: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory.

deadlines.title: Environmental monitoring swabs
deadlines.source_line: Listeria spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2

deadlines.title: Environmental monitoring trend review
deadlines.source_line: Environmental monitoring results are trended quarterly.

deadlines.title: Metal detector test-piece checks
deadlines.source_line: The line lead runs the three metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records the result.

deadlines.title: Employee food hygiene training
deadlines.source_line: All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually.

deadlines.title: Plan reanalysis (inferred from the rule; not stated in the document)
deadlines.source_line: Not in the document. Worked out from 21 CFR 117.170(a) (at least every 3 years) and the "Effective date: May 12, 2025"

facts.quote: for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho
facts.affects: Product crosses state lines, so FDA jurisdiction applies clearly; this also sets recall notification scope.

facts.value: One shift, five days a week
facts.quote: The Salem plant operates one shift, five days a week
facts.affects: Sets monitoring and environmental swab timing, and the sanitation and changeover windows.
Places the company well under 500 full-time equivalent employees (a small business under Part 117). Whether it is a very small business depends on sales, which the plan does not state.
Long refrigerated RTE shelf life makes Listeria growth control and shelf-life validation central.

facts.value: Refrigerated RTE hummus and bean dips (chickpea or black bean), in 8-oz and 16-oz sealed plastic tubs
facts.quote: produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-ounce sealed plastic tubs
facts.affects: RTE product exposed after the kill step, which brings environmental monitoring and sanitation controls into play.

facts.quote: Products are labeled with the allergen statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
facts.affects: Requires allergen cross-contact and labeling controls for non-sesame bean dips run on shared equipment.

facts.value: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager (FSPCA PCQI course, March 2024)
facts.quote: Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
facts.affects: The named PCQI is responsible for preparing the plan, validation, records review and reanalysis.

Citations are to 21 CFR Part 117 from my own knowledge of the rule. I did not re-check them against eCFR for this reading, but these sections have been stable. One gap is new: cooling monitoring has no start time. It is my inference about whether the monitoring is adequate. Also inferred, and worth confirming with the plant: whether the 212°F internal cook limit is physically reachable in the kettle at Salem's elevation, and what supports the 45-day shelf life (pH or preservatives are not mentioned). I did not assess whether the products fall under FDA's Food Traceability List rule (FSMA 204). That needs a separate check.

FOOD SAFETY PLAN
Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
Salem Plant, 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301
Effective date: May 12, 2025
Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
(PCQI certificate, FSPCA course, March 2024)
Approved by: Plant Manager
1. Facility and product description
Willamette Valley Foods produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-
ounce sealed plastic tubs for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. The Salem plant operates one
shift, five days a week, with 28 production employees. Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black
beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices, blended, filled, sealed, coded and held
refrigerated at or below 41°F. Shelf life is 45 days refrigerated. Products are labeled with the allergen
statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
2. Process flow
Receiving of dry beans, tahini and other ingredients → dry storage or refrigerated storage → soaking and
cooking of beans (kettle, 212°F, 60 minutes minimum) → cooling in the blast chiller → blending with
other ingredients → filling and sealing → date coding → metal detection → refrigerated storage →
shipping.

5. Monitoring
The kettle operator records the internal temperature and the time at the start and end of each cook batch
on the cook log. The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling
log. The sanitation lead records the ATP swab result before each start-up. The line lead runs the three
metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records
the result. The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs
the label log.
6. Corrective actions
If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or
discarded, and the cause is recorded. If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. If an ATP
swab fails, the surface is re-cleaned and re-swabbed before production starts. If a Listeria spp. swab is
positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since
the last negative swab is held pending investigation. If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product
since the last passing test is re-run through the detector. If a label does not match the formulation, the lot
is quarantined and not used. All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed
by the PCQI within seven days.
7. Verification
The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven
working days of their creation. Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,
and the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually. Finished product is tested for Listeria
monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended
quarterly.
8. Supply-chain program
Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit
certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The approved supplier list is maintained by the quality
manager.
9. Records
All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record
and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request. Records are reviewed and
signed by the PCQI as described in section 7.
10. Training
All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current
FSPCA certificate. Sanitation and line leads are trained on the monitoring procedures in this plan.
